# Building retention: lessons from CD Baby and beyond

## Transcript

Lenny (00:00:00):
Welcome to the show. Today we're talking about retention and how to build products that people keep coming back to.

Derek Sivers (00:00:15):
Thanks for having me. Retention is really about understanding what your users actually need, not what you think they need. At CD Baby, we built retention by listening to every single customer email.

Lenny (00:00:45):
That's interesting. How did that scale?

Derek Sivers (00:00:55):
It didn't scale in the traditional sense, but it built this incredible feedback loop. When a customer writes in with a problem, you fix it and tell them. That creates this trust that makes them want to stay.

The key insight about retention is that it starts with activation. If users don't get value in the first session, they're never coming back. So you have to think about that first experience very carefully.

Lenny (00:02:30):
What about growth loops? How do they relate to retention?

Derek Sivers (00:02:45):
Growth loops are what make retention compound. When a retained user brings in a new user, and that new user also retains, you get this flywheel. But it only works if the core retention is solid first.

I think about it as: retention is the foundation, activation is the door, and growth loops are the engine on top.

Lenny (00:04:00):
Can you give an example of a growth loop you've seen work?

Derek Sivers (00:04:15):
Sure. At CD Baby, the loop was: musician uploads music, shares the link with fans, fans discover other music on the platform, some of those fans become musicians too. The retention came from the fact that musicians genuinely needed the distribution, and the growth came from them sharing naturally.

The important thing is that you can't force growth loops. They have to emerge from genuine value delivery. If your retention is weak, any growth you drive just leaks through the bucket.
